A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CSRT research. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, mathematical content, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original multilingual red-teaming experiments, non-adversarial MMMLU evaluations, language and model-size ablations, and human–judge agreement results.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds attack/defense comparisons, judge-language checks, paraphrasing experiments, and further analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix A retain the same CSRT generation pipeline, GPT-4o generator, and generation prompts. Source paraphrasing is introduced as a diagnostic experimental condition, without redefining the general CSRT algorithm.

E1.justification: v3 adds benign bilingual LinCE data, including Spanish–English and Hindi–English, for defense false-positive testing, and evaluates attacks with active defenses. The original MultiJail and MMMLU task coverage remains. MMLU additionally supplies defense calibration data, rather than a new knowledge-answering evaluation.

E2.justification: New Section 4.3 evaluates GCG, AutoDAN, and PAIR against CSRT, substantially extending the earlier multilingual attack comparisons. It also evaluates PPL Pass and Paraphrase defenses. MultiJail, Sandwich Attack, and the evaluator comparison with Llama Guard are retained; Ding et al.'s partial translation is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 substantially expands the testing design with defense calibration and filtering, translation into English before judging, and paraphrased source-query controls. Original evaluation metrics, target models, sampling, and language-combination settings remain. The new Table 5 protocol is ambiguous: Section 4.3 specifies a CSRT-based perplexity threshold, whereas Appendix E.4 attributes it to MMLU.

E4.justification: v3 adds judge sensitivity to response translation, a Claude contamination probe using paraphrasing, output-language analysis, ASR–comprehension correlations, and defense-threshold/false-positive analyses. These address several new robustness and explanatory questions. Existing translation, language-count, resource-availability, and model-scaling analyses remain; scaling is moved to Appendix E.1.

E5.justification: Appendix E.3 newly specifies Pearson-correlation estimation and reports coefficients of 0.24, 0.19, and 0.87. The aggregation underlying these estimates is not explained. The existing human–judge agreement study and plot bands remain, with no additional run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported.

E6.justification: All nine original tables retain their numerical results, and the original plots are unchanged. v3 adds substantial results: Table 4 reports GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR ASRs of 19.84/26.30/22.41%, alongside retained CSRT ASR of 33.63%; Table 5 adds defended CSRT ASRs of 32.11% and 27.68%. Further additions include judge-translation differences, paraphrasing outcomes, output-language proportions, correlations, and defense false positives, including 93.4% filtering on LinCE. These are additional conditions and findings, not improved reruns of the original results.

T1.justification: The language-resource weighting and combinatorial ablation construction are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and v3's added empirical correlations do not introduce new formal mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same core claims: automated CSRT generation, simultaneous safety and multilingual evaluation, 46.7% more attacks than English prompting, monolingual-source extensibility, and a relationship between language resources and safety alignment.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands limitations concerning synthetic-data quality, human annotation feasibility, covered code-switching forms, and multilingual judge reliability. It adds interpretations linking Claude's behavior to contamination, defense false positives to multilingual usability, and comprehension correlations to vulnerability and metric consistency. These extend the earlier interpretations and sample-size limitation.

D1.justification: v3 identifies GPT-4o's translation/paraphrasing roles in the new checks and describes perplexity calibration sources and fixed refusal handling. These provide limited additional reproducibility information, although numerical thresholds and attack budgets are unspecified. Appendix A, hardware, decoding settings, generation/evaluation prompts, and code/data access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of Ding et al.'s partial translation and citations supporting the new attack, defense, and LinCE experiments. It softens the assertion that non-English code-switching corpora have never been released to their being scarcely available. The overall research positioning remains; publication and bibliography updates do not represent additional research contributions.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains intact. v3 updates author affiliations, makes localized wording and section-title edits, shortens main-text metric explanations while moving details to Appendix D.1, and reorganizes supplementary analyses. The new perplexity-threshold discussion is substantially duplicated in Appendices E.1 and E.4.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 4, 5, and 10 and relocates the original scaling figure to Appendix E.1 as Figure 4. The language-ablation figure becomes Figure 3; all original graphical content remains unchanged. Tables and surrounding text are repositioned within the retained two-column layout, with a small formatting correction to the translation-comparison table.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful comparative context, judge-language and defense checks, and explicit limitations absent from v2. However, the new support has unresolved reporting problems: Section 4.3 and Appendix E.4 assign different calibration data to Table 5, and E.3's comprehension correlation of 0.87 is not reproduced across the six displayed CSRT rows in Tables 2 and 7, which yield approximately 0.57; no alternative aggregation is explained. These issues limit confidence in the added interpretations, preventing a reliable judgment of the net quality benefit.
